planting.note: Direct sow in late summer for a fall/winter crop, or 4-6 weeks before last spring frost; repeat-sow every few weeks for continuous harvest.

directions: Scatter seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil and thin to about a foot apart; this Asian green is a cross between tatsoi and komatsuna, forming a tight rosette of glossy, savoyed dark-green leaves with a mild, velvety texture. It holds up to both summer heat and hard frost better than plain tatsoi, so it can anchor a garden through most of the cool season, and it tolerates part shade in warm climates without losing vigor. Harvest outer leaves continually or cut the whole rosette at the base; younger leaves eaten raw make a good spinach substitute, while larger leaves are best quickly sauteed or added to soups.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for a fall/winter crop in mild climates; thin to final spacing once seedlings have true leaves.

directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in rows a foot apart in rich, well-drained soil; Barese is a traditional Italian chard valued for exceptionally tender, delicate leaves and ribs that stay sweet rather than turning tough or bitter even as plants size up. It can be cut young as baby greens or left to grow into full heads, and tolerates both heat and a bit of shade better than many lettuce substitutes. Harvest outer leaves from the base while leaving the center intact so the plant keeps resprouting through the season; frost actually sweetens the flavor of late-season leaves.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or sow in late summer about 50 days before first fall frost for a fall crop.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep directly in the garden or start in trays for later transplant; Green Mountain produces an especially large, jumbo central stalk that stays crisp and juicy, with a flavor many compare to cucumber crossed with sweet corn. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest once the stalk has swollen to an inch or more across but before the plant bolts, since heat and flowering quickly turn the stem pithy and bitter. Peel the tough outer skin before eating the stalk raw in salads, stir-fried, or shredded as a pasta substitute; young outer leaves are edible too.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last spring frost, or 4-7 weeks before first fall frost; in mild Gulf Coast winters can be grown through the cool season for a late-fall to winter harvest.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Manoa was bred at the University of Hawaii for heat tolerance and forms full, uniform heads of tender, sweet-flavored leaves that resist the quick bolting typical of butterhead types in warm weather. Growing it with afternoon shade or shade cloth through the hottest months helps keep the heads from turning bitter. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pick outer leaves individually for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall/winter crop, or 4-6 weeks before last spring frost; sweetens after a touch of frost.

directions: Sow seed 1/4-1/2 inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-prostrate North Carolina heirloom, preserved by the Prevatte and Britt families near Lumberton and later shared through the Heirloom Collard Project, has a moderate tendency to form a loose cabbage-like head. Its sweet, tender yellow-green leaves carry a nutty, cabbage-like flavor that is less pungent than many collard types, and the plants are vigorous and hardy to around 20°F. Harvest outer leaves continuously through fall and winter, or cut the loosely headed center once it firms up; flavor improves noticeably after frost.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or direct sow in late summer for a fall/winter crop; a late-fall or winter harvest after frost gives the sweetest flavor.

directions: Sow seed 1/4-1/2 inch deep in fertile soil and thin or transplant to final spacing; this rare North Carolina heirloom was kept for generations by farmer William Alexander of Columbia, NC and selected specifically for its slight heading habit, giving broad, wavy, deep-green leaves that curl inward to form a loose, cabbage-like center while outer leaves stay loose. The flavor is rich and distinctly mustardy with a touch of sweetness, more assertive than milder collard types. Harvest outer leaves as needed through the season, or cut the compact center head once it firms; like other collards it is more cold-hardy than cabbage and improves in flavor after frost.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 60°F, ideally 70-90°F; this vigorous pole lima needs a sturdy trellis and thrives through Gulf Coast summer heat and drought.

directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep and space about 6 inches apart along a tall trellis in full sun; this Alabama family heirloom butterbean is a true lima bean prized for creamy white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye and for outstanding heat and drought tolerance once established. Avoid soaking seed before planting, as it can cause rot in warm, moist soil. Keep moisture consistent through flowering and pod set, and harvest pods once plump for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for storage beans.

planting.note: Direct sow 3-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed past 60°F; this tall pole lima needs a sturdy trellis and a long, hot season to mature its large seeds.

directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep along a trellis tall enough for 10-foot vines, in well-drained soil enriched with compost; Christmas Pole, also known regionally as Christmas Lima or Chestnut Lima, traces back to Lima, Peru and produces large, flat seeds nearly 3/4 inch across packed into 4-6 inch pods. Cooked seeds have a rich, chestnut-like flavor and texture that historically made the variety a holiday substitute for chestnuts. Grow in consistently warm, moist soil through the full length of summer, and harvest pods once plump for fresh shelling or allow them to dry on the vine for long-term storage beans.
